transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi… yeah. I’m here mostly because my sleep has just kind of fallen apart. I keep thinking I’m going to get into bed and finally shut my brain off, but I’ll be lying there in my apartment for hours, and my laptop is closed, like I’m technically done working, but mentally I’m still going through everything.

It’s like I’m rechecking work deadlines in my head, then I’ll suddenly think about tuition payments, then class assignments, and then I loop back around to work again. I’ll tell myself, “Okay, stop, you already handled that,” but it doesn’t really stop. And even on the nights when I do fall asleep, I wake up feeling like I never actually rested—like I never fully turned off. It’s been really exhausting.
Do you find yourself feeling anxious or worried during the day, even when you're not trying to fall asleep?

Yeah, definitely. It’s not just at night. During the day it’s like my brain is constantly scanning for something I should be worried about. I’ll be at work and start thinking, “Am I falling behind? Did I miss something? Is this going to make me look incompetent?” And then even if nothing actually happened, I’ll jump to thinking about school and whether I’m wasting money on tuition if I can’t keep up the way I’m supposed to.

And then it turns into this whole bigger thing, like… if I struggle with one assignment or one deadline, suddenly my mind is acting like that means my whole future is going to fall apart. I’ll think about my family and whether they’re going to see me as someone who can’t handle things, or like I made all these choices and now I’m failing at them. It’s embarrassing because sometimes the thing that starts it is really small, but in my head it feels like proof that everything is on the edge of derailing.
Do you feel like your worrying is something you can’t control, even when you try to stop thinking about things?

Yeah… very much. That’s actually one of the most frustrating parts, because I’ll be aware that I’m doing it. Like I’ll literally tell myself, “Okay, stop. Just focus on the one thing in front of you.” But it doesn’t feel like my brain listens.

I’ll start with one worry, like a work deadline, and then almost immediately it turns into, “Wait, what about that thing on my calendar?” So I check my calendar. Then while I’m checking that, I remember something about money or tuition or my budget, so I open that too. And then somehow I’m thinking about assignments, and whether I missed something there, so I go check that again.

It becomes this loop where I’m not even solving anything anymore. I’m just checking the same things over and over—calendar, budget, assignments, work stuff—and I keep thinking if I check one more time I’ll feel settled, but I don’t. I just lose a ton of time and then realize I haven’t actually gotten anything done, which makes me worry even more. So yes, it really does feel out of my control.
When you're feeling this worry or anxiety, do you notice any physical symptoms, like a racing heart, sweating, shaking, or feeling tense?

I’m not totally sure, honestly. I mean, I know I feel anxious, but I don’t always know how to separate what’s “physical” from just… being worked up in my head, if that makes sense.

I don’t think I’ve really noticed sweating or shaking in a clear way. And I’m not sure about my heart racing—I don’t usually stop and check my pulse or anything. Sometimes I’m so focused on the worry itself that I only realize afterward that I’ve been kind of bracing myself, but I don’t know if that counts as feeling tense or if I’m just stressed.

So… I guess the honest answer is I haven’t paid close enough attention to say for sure. I mostly notice the thoughts and the inability to settle down more than specific body symptoms.
Do you find yourself feeling restless or unable to relax, even when there’s no specific reason to worry?

I’m not sure how to answer that cleanly, because I don’t always know what counts as “no specific reason.” Like, if I’m restless, my mind usually finds a reason pretty quickly, even if it’s kind of vague or not actually urgent.

I do have times where I feel like I should be able to just sit down and relax, and I can’t really settle into it. But I don’t know if that’s because there’s truly nothing to worry about, or because I’m already sort of keyed up and then I start looking for something that explains it. Like I’ll sit on the couch and think, “Okay, I’m done for the day, I can just watch something,” but then I’m still kind of… mentally hovering, I guess. Not necessarily pacing around or anything dramatic, just not fully relaxed.

So I guess I’d say I’ve noticed trouble relaxing, but I’m not totally sure whether it happens without a reason, because it feels like there’s almost always some possible reason my brain can attach to.
Do you find that you have trouble concentrating or focusing on tasks because your mind is preoccupied with worries?

Yes, definitely. That’s actually one of the main ways it messes with me day to day. I’ll be trying to do something that should be pretty straightforward, like working on a financial model for work, and I’ll just… freeze on the same part. I’m looking at the numbers, I know technically what I’m supposed to be doing, but my mind is already somewhere else running through every possible thing that could go wrong.

Or with class readings, I’ll read the same paragraph over and over—like five times—and then realize I have no idea what it said. Not because it’s too hard, necessarily, but because while my eyes are moving across the page, my brain is thinking about whether I missed something, or if I’m behind, or if one thing going badly is going to make everything else fall apart.

It’s frustrating because from the outside it probably just looks like I’m being inefficient or distracted, but internally it feels like I’m trying to concentrate through this constant background noise. I’ll keep dragging myself back to the task, and then a minute later I’m off in my head again, going through all these scenarios. So yes, my focus is pretty badly affected.
Do you find that you feel fatigued or low on energy most days, even if you’ve had some sleep?

Yes. That’s actually been happening a lot. By the middle of the afternoon at work, I can feel just completely wiped out, like I hit a wall. And it’s not just normal “I could use a coffee” tired — it’s more like even small things start feeling weirdly effortful. Answering emails, switching between tasks, getting up to go to the bathroom, even thinking about walking to the subway after work can feel like this huge thing I have to gear myself up for.

And I do sleep some, so it’s not like I’m awake all night every night or something. But even when I’ve slept, I don’t really feel restored. I keep thinking, “Okay, if I just make it to the weekend and rest, I’ll reset,” but then the weekend comes and I’ll rest, or try to, and by Monday I don’t feel like I’ve gotten my energy back in any meaningful way. It’s frustrating because I feel like I’m constantly running on a low battery, and then the regular parts of the day take way more out of me than they should.
Have you noticed yourself becoming more irritable or easily annoyed, especially when you're feeling tired or overwhelmed?

I’m not completely sure, honestly. I mean, I can get annoyed like anyone else, but I don’t know that I’ve specifically noticed a big change where I’m suddenly snapping at people or anything like that.

When I’m tired or overwhelmed, I think I’m more… short internally, if that makes sense. Like things feel harder to tolerate, and I may have less patience for interruptions or unexpected requests. But I don’t know if other people would describe me as irritable, because I usually try pretty hard to keep it contained and not show it. Sometimes I’ll notice myself thinking, “Why is this person asking me this right now?” when it’s probably a totally normal question.

So maybe there’s some of that, but I wouldn’t say it’s the main thing I’ve noticed, or at least I haven’t paid as much attention to it as I have to the tiredness and trouble focusing.
Do you find that you worry about a wide range of things, even when they’re not necessarily that important or urgent?

Yes. Very much so. It’s not even like there’s one huge crisis I’m responding to — it’s more like my mind is constantly scanning for things to be worried about, and it jumps around between them all day.

Like, I’ll start off worrying that I’m falling behind at work, even if I’m technically meeting deadlines, because I’ll think, “What if I’m missing something obvious? What if someone realizes I’m not doing enough?” And then somehow that turns into worrying about school, like whether I’m wasting money on it or whether I made the wrong decision, and then that turns into worrying about my family thinking I can’t handle things or that I’m not as put together as I should be at 29.

And the thing is, a lot of these things are not urgent in the moment. Sometimes they’re not even actual problems yet. But they feel urgent in my head. Like a small issue doesn’t stay small — if I make one mistake on something, my brain immediately treats it like it could set off this whole chain reaction and derail my entire future. I know that sounds dramatic when I say it out loud, but in the moment it feels very real, like I have to solve everything right then or I’m going to fall apart somehow.
Have you noticed yourself feeling down, hopeless, or losing interest in things you usually enjoy, even for short periods during the day?

I’m not really sure. I don’t think hopeless is the word I’d use, at least not in a clear way. I do have moments where I feel kind of discouraged or flat, especially if I’ve been thinking too much about everything I need to handle, but I don’t know that I’d describe it as feeling depressed, exactly.

As far as losing interest in things, I mean… sometimes I don’t feel like doing much, but it’s hard for me to tell whether that’s because I’ve lost interest or because I’m just tired and mentally drained. Like if a friend suggests something after work, I might think, “That sounds like too much,” even if normally I’d enjoy seeing them. But I don’t know if that counts as not enjoying things, because if I actually get myself there, I can sometimes still have an okay time.

So I guess I’d say I haven’t really noticed a strong pattern of feeling hopeless or not caring about anything. It’s more that my mood can dip for a bit when I’m overwhelmed, but I’m not sure I’d call it that.
Have you found that you take less pleasure in activities you used to enjoy, even for short periods during the day?

I’m honestly not sure I’d say “less pleasure,” exactly. I’ve thought about that a little because it’s hard to separate enjoyment from just being tired or preoccupied.

Like, there are things I normally like — watching a show, going out to eat with a friend, doing something low-key after work — and sometimes they don’t sound appealing in the moment. But it’s not always because I don’t enjoy them anymore. It’s more like the effort of starting feels like a lot, or I’m already mentally somewhere else, so I’m not as excited about it as I think I should be.

If I actually do the thing, I can still enjoy it at least somewhat. Maybe not always fully, because my mind can be distracted, but I don’t think I’ve had this clear sense of, “Nothing is enjoyable anymore.” It’s more inconsistent than that. Some moments I’m engaged and fine, and other times I’m just sort of going through the motions because I’m worn out. So… I don’t know. I haven’t noticed a definite loss of pleasure, if that’s what you mean.
Have you had days where you feel down or sad most of the time, even when there’s nothing specific going on to explain it?

I don’t think so, not in the sense of being sad most of the day for no clear reason. I mean, I do have times where I feel kind of low or emotionally worn down, but usually when I really think about it, it’s tied to feeling overwhelmed or like I’ve been carrying too much in my head.

It’s not like I wake up and the whole day just feels sad for no reason, if that makes sense. More often it’s like my mood gets pulled down after I’ve been thinking about responsibilities or things I’m worried I’m not handling well. And then I might feel discouraged for a while, or quieter than usual, or like I don’t have much energy to be upbeat. But I wouldn’t say it’s most of the day, and I wouldn’t say it comes out of nowhere.

I guess I’m a little unsure where the line is, because sometimes the reason isn’t one obvious event — it’s more like a buildup. But no, I haven’t really noticed days where I’m just sad most of the time without something behind it.
Do you often have trouble falling asleep because your thoughts are racing or you can't shut them off, even when you're physically tired?

Yes. That’s actually one of the main reasons I’m here, because my sleep has basically fallen apart.

I’ll be physically exhausted — like, I can feel that my body is tired — and I’ll get into bed in my apartment, close my laptop, lights off or mostly off, and then my brain just keeps going. It’s not even always one big dramatic thought. It’s more like I start mentally rechecking everything: work deadlines, emails I might have missed, whether I handled something correctly, then tuition payments, then class assignments, then I remember some other thing I need to do, and it just keeps looping.

And the frustrating part is I’ll tell myself, “Okay, you’re done for the day, you need to sleep,” but it doesn’t feel like there’s an off switch. I can be lying there for hours, not doing anything, not even on my computer anymore, but still kind of working in my head. And then even when I do finally fall asleep, it doesn’t feel restful. I wake up feeling like I never really turned off, like my mind was still running in the background the whole time.
Do you notice any tightness in your muscles, especially in your neck, shoulders, or back, even when you're not doing anything physically strenuous?

I’m not totally sure. I mean, I know what you mean in a general sense, like carrying tension in your shoulders or clenching without realizing it, but I haven’t really tracked that carefully.

I do sometimes notice I’m sort of… held stiffly, I guess, like I’ll realize I’m sitting at my desk with my shoulders up or my posture is really rigid. But I don’t know if I’d call it muscle tightness as a symptom, exactly, because I also sit at a computer a lot for work, so it’s hard for me to separate what’s just from being at my desk versus something else.

My neck and shoulders can feel tense at times, but I haven’t had this clear ongoing back or neck pain that I’ve been focused on. It’s more like I notice it after the fact, like, “Oh, I’m not relaxed,” but I wouldn’t say I’ve been doing anything physically strenuous when it happens. I just haven’t paid enough attention to say how often it’s happening.
Do you often have trouble falling asleep because your thoughts are racing or you can't shut them off, even when you're physically tired?

Yes — definitely. Honestly, that’s one of the biggest reasons I’m here, because my sleep has basically fallen apart.

I’ll be lying in bed in my apartment, physically tired, laptop already closed, trying to be done for the day, and my mind just keeps going. I start rechecking things in my head — work deadlines, whether I missed something, tuition payments, class assignments — and it just loops. It’s like I can’t convince my brain that it’s allowed to stop.

Sometimes I’ll be there for hours, not even doing anything, just lying there thinking through the same things again and again. And then even when I do finally sleep, I wake up feeling like I never really turned off. It doesn’t feel restful.
Do you often feel excessively sleepy or struggle to stay awake during the day, even after what you think should have been a full night's sleep?

Yeah, I do. I don’t know if I’d describe it as, like, literally nodding off at my desk all the time, but I feel really drained during the day. By midafternoon at the office, it’s like I hit this wall where even small things feel weirdly hard — answering emails, responding to messages, getting through whatever task I’m supposed to be doing.

And it’s not just “I could use a coffee” tired. It feels like my whole body and brain are running on empty. Even walking to the subway after work can feel like this huge effort, which sounds dramatic, but that’s how it feels in the moment.

I keep thinking if I could just catch up on sleep or rest on the weekend, I’d bounce back, but that doesn’t really happen. I’ll try to take it easy, and then Monday comes and I still feel like I’m starting the week already depleted. So yes, during the day I’m tired a lot — more drained than sleepy maybe, but definitely struggling to feel awake and functional.
Do you find it hard to get started on tasks or responsibilities, even when you know you need to do them, because it feels like there’s no motivation or energy to begin?

Yes, I do. It’s not even always that I don’t care about the task — like, I know the email needs an answer, or I know I need to start something for work — but by midafternoon at the office I feel so completely drained that starting feels weirdly impossible.

Even small things can feel like they require this huge amount of effort. I’ll be sitting there looking at my inbox thinking, “Okay, just answer this one message,” and it still feels like I have to force myself through mud to begin. And then by the time I’m leaving work, even something basic like walking to the subway can feel like more effort than it should.

I keep hoping that if I rest over the weekend, I’ll sort of reset and come back with more energy, but it doesn’t really work that way. I might take it easy, but I don’t feel restored enough. It’s like I’m starting from empty again.
Do you find yourself moving more slowly than usual, or having trouble thinking clearly and making decisions, even when you're not physically tired?

Yes — mostly the thinking clearly and making decisions part. I’m not sure I’d say I’m physically moving in slow motion all the time, but mentally I get really stuck.

Like I’ll be looking at the same financial model at work, something I technically know how to review, and I’ll just… stare at it. I’ll read the same numbers or assumptions over and over and realize I haven’t actually taken anything in. Or with class readings, I’ll get through a paragraph and then notice I’ve basically reread the same paragraph five times and still couldn’t tell you what it said.

And it’s not because the material is impossible. It’s more like my mind is already somewhere else, running through everything that could go wrong — what if I miss something in the model, what if I fall behind, what if I don’t understand the reading well enough — and then I’m technically looking at the task, but I’m not really there. Even small decisions can take way longer than they should because I keep second-guessing what the “right” choice is.
Have you been worrying about multiple things in your life, like work, school, or personal responsibilities, for more days than not over the past six months or longer?

Yes. Honestly, that’s probably the main thing that’s been going on. It’s not just one worry that comes and goes — my mind keeps jumping between different things, and it feels constant.

Like I’ll start out worrying that I’m falling behind at work, that I’m missing something important or not keeping up the way I’m supposed to. Then it turns into worrying about school and whether I’m wasting money on it, or whether I made the wrong choice trying to do all of this. And then somehow it becomes about my family and whether they’re going to think I can’t handle my life or that I’m not as capable as I should be.

It’s like every small issue feels bigger than it probably is. One email I haven’t answered, one assignment I’m unsure about, one expense I didn’t plan for — my brain treats it like it could derail everything, like my whole future is suddenly at risk. I know that sounds extreme when I say it out loud, but in the moment it feels very real. So yes, more days than not, for a long time now, I’m worrying about multiple things at once.

Not because it’s too hard, necessarily, but because while my eyes are moving across the page, my brain is thinking about whether I missed something, or if I’m behind, or if one thing going badly is going to make everything else fall apart.

It’s frustrating because from the outside it probably just looks like I’m being inefficient or distracted, but internally it feels like I’m trying to concentrate through this constant background noise. I’ll keep dragging myself back to the task, and then a minute later I’m off in my head again, going through all these scenarios. So yes, my focus is pretty badly affected.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences symptoms of fatigue or low energy nearly every day, which would help differentiate between GAD (F41.1), Adjustment Disorder with Anxiety (F43.22), and Primary Insomnia (F51.0).
doctor.question: Do you find that you feel fatigued or low on energy most days, even if you’ve had some sleep?

target_item.name: Fatigue
target_item.manifestation: By midafternoon at the office I feel completely drained, like even answering emails or walking to the subway takes effort, and resting on the weekend doesn’t seem to give me my energy back.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking about feeling fatigued or low on energy despite having some sleep.

patient.answer:
Yes. That’s actually been happening a lot. By the middle of the afternoon at work, I can feel just completely wiped out, like I hit a wall. And it’s not just normal “I could use a coffee” tired — it’s more like even small things start feeling weirdly effortful. Answering emails, switching between tasks, getting up to go to the bathroom, even thinking about walking to the subway after work can feel like this huge thing I have to gear myself up for.

And I do sleep some, so it’s not like I’m awake all night every night or something. But even when I’ve slept, I don’t really feel restored. I keep thinking, “Okay, if I just make it to the weekend and rest, I’ll reset,” but then the weekend comes and I’ll rest, or try to, and by Monday I don’t feel like I’ve gotten my energy back in any meaningful way. It’s frustrating because I feel like I’m constantly running on a low battery, and then the regular parts of the day take way more out of me than they should.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences symptoms of irritability related to their anxiety and fatigue, which could help differentiate between GAD (F41.1), Adjustment Disorder with Anxiety (F43.22), or another condition.
doctor.question: Have you noticed yourself becoming more irritable or easily annoyed, especially when you're feeling tired or overwhelmed?

target_item.reason: The question is directly about irritability or being easily annoyed, which is not covered by any listed symptom profile. Although it mentions feeling tired or overwhelmed, the main symptom being asked about is irritability, not fatigue or worry.

patient.answer:
I’m not completely sure, honestly. I mean, I can get annoyed like anyone else, but I don’t know that I’ve specifically noticed a big change where I’m suddenly snapping at people or anything like that.

When I’m tired or overwhelmed, I think I’m more… short internally, if that makes sense. Like things feel harder to tolerate, and I may have less patience for interruptions or unexpected requests. But I don’t know if other people would describe me as irritable, because I usually try pretty hard to keep it contained and not show it. Sometimes I’ll notice myself thinking, “Why is this person asking me this right now?” when it’s probably a totally normal question.

So maybe there’s some of that, but I wouldn’t say it’s the main thing I’ve noticed, or at least I haven’t paid as much attention to it as I have to the tiredness and trouble focusing.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences excessive worry about a variety of events or activities (generalized anxiety), which would support F41.1 over other candidates.
doctor.question: Do you find that you worry about a wide range of things, even when they’re not necessarily that important or urgent?

target_item.name: Excessive_Anxiety_Worry
target_item.manifestation: My mind keeps jumping from whether I’m falling behind at work, to whether I’m wasting money on school, to whether my family will think I can’t handle things, and I treat every small issue like it could derail my whole future.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the worry spans a wide range of topics and is disproportionate to their urgency or importance, which directly matches excessive anxiety and worry about multiple events or activities.

patient.answer:
Yes. Very much so. It’s not even like there’s one huge crisis I’m responding to — it’s more like my mind is constantly scanning for things to be worried about, and it jumps around between them all day.

Like, I’ll start off worrying that I’m falling behind at work, even if I’m technically meeting deadlines, because I’ll think, “What if I’m missing something obvious? What if someone realizes I’m not doing enough?” And then somehow that turns into worrying about school, like whether I’m wasting money on it or whether I made the wrong decision, and then that turns into worrying about my family thinking I can’t handle things or that I’m not as put together as I should be at 29.

And the thing is, a lot of these things are not urgent in the moment. Sometimes they’re not even actual problems yet. But they feel urgent in my head. Like a small issue doesn’t stay small — if I make one mistake on something, my brain immediately treats it like it could set off this whole chain reaction and derail my entire future. I know that sounds dramatic when I say it out loud, but in the moment it feels very real, like I have to solve everything right then or I’m going to fall apart somehow.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences symptoms of depression, specifically persistent low mood or loss of interest in activities, to differentiate between GAD (F41.1), Adjustment Disorder with Anxiety (F51.0), and Major Depressive Disorder (F43.22).
doctor.question: Have you noticed yourself feeling down, hopeless, or losing interest in things you usually enjoy, even for short periods during the day?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about depressive mood, hopelessness, or loss of interest/anhedonia, which is not covered by the provided symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
I’m not really sure. I don’t think hopeless is the word I’d use, at least not in a clear way. I do have moments where I feel kind of discouraged or flat, especially if I’ve been thinking too much about everything I need to handle, but I don’t know that I’d describe it as feeling depressed, exactly.

As far as losing interest in things, I mean… sometimes I don’t feel like doing much, but it’s hard for me to tell whether that’s because I’ve lost interest or because I’m just tired and mentally drained. Like if a friend suggests something after work, I might think, “That sounds like too much,” even if normally I’d enjoy seeing them. But I don’t know if that counts as not enjoying things, because if I actually get myself there, I can sometimes still have an okay time.

So I guess I’d say I haven’t really noticed a strong pattern of feeling hopeless or not caring about anything. It’s more that my mood can dip for a bit when I’m overwhelmed, but I’m not sure I’d call it that.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences symptoms of depression, specifically anhedonia, to differentiate between Generalized Anxiety Disorder (F41.1), Adjustment Disorder with Anxiety (F51.0), and Anxiety Disorder due to Another Medical Condition (F43.22).
doctor.question: Have you found that you take less pleasure in activities you used to enjoy, even for short periods during the day?

target_item.reason: The question is specifically about reduced pleasure or anhedonia, which is not covered by the provided symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
I’m honestly not sure I’d say “less pleasure,” exactly. I’ve thought about that a little because it’s hard to separate enjoyment from just being tired or preoccupied.

Like, there are things I normally like — watching a show, going out to eat with a friend, doing something low-key after work — and sometimes they don’t sound appealing in the moment. But it’s not always because I don’t enjoy them anymore. It’s more like the effort of starting feels like a lot, or I’m already mentally somewhere else, so I’m not as excited about it as I think I should be.

If I actually do the thing, I can still enjoy it at least somewhat. Maybe not always fully, because my mind can be distracted, but I don’t think I’ve had this clear sense of, “Nothing is enjoyable anymore.” It’s more inconsistent than that. Some moments I’m engaged and fine, and other times I’m just sort of going through the motions because I’m worn out. So… I don’t know. I haven’t noticed a definite loss of pleasure, if that’s what you mean.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences symptoms of low mood or anhedonia that may support a diagnosis of major depressive disorder (F41.1) versus other candidates.
doctor.question: Have you had days where you feel down or sad most of the time, even when there’s nothing specific going on to explain it?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about persistent down or sad mood, which is a depressive mood symptom not covered by the provided generalized anxiety symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
I don’t think so, not in the sense of being sad most of the day for no clear reason. I mean, I do have times where I feel kind of low or emotionally worn down, but usually when I really think about it, it’s tied to feeling overwhelmed or like I’ve been carrying too much in my head.

It’s not like I wake up and the whole day just feels sad for no reason, if that makes sense. More often it’s like my mood gets pulled down after I’ve been thinking about responsibilities or things I’m worried I’m not handling well. And then I might feel discouraged for a while, or quieter than usual, or like I don’t have much energy to be upbeat. But I wouldn’t say it’s most of the day, and I wouldn’t say it comes out of nowhere.

I guess I’m a little unsure where the line is, because sometimes the reason isn’t one obvious event — it’s more like a buildup. But no, I haven’t really noticed days where I’m just sad most of the time without something behind it.

inference.note: The patient continues to endorse core features of Generalized Anxiety Disorder (F41.1), including excessive worry about multiple domains, difficulty controlling worry, and associated symptoms such as fatigue, concentration problems, and restlessness. No new information has emerged to definitively rule out Adjustment Disorder with Anxiety (F43.22) or Nonorganic Insomnia (F51.0), as there is overlap in symptoms across these conditions. The presentation remains most consistent with F41.1, but the differential remains open.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences difficulty falling asleep due to racing thoughts, which is a key distinguishing feature between the remaining diagnostic candidates.
doctor.question: Do you often have trouble falling asleep because your thoughts are racing or you can't shut them off, even when you're physically tired?

target_item.name: Sleep_Disturbance
target_item.manifestation: I’m here because my sleep has basically fallen apart—I’ll lie in bed in my apartment for hours with my laptop closed, still mentally rechecking work deadlines, tuition payments, and class assignments, and even when I do sleep I wake up feeling like I never really turned off.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking directly about difficulty falling asleep due to racing thoughts, which matches the sleep disturbance symptom.

patient.answer:
Yes. That’s actually one of the main reasons I’m here, because my sleep has basically fallen apart.

I’ll be physically exhausted — like, I can feel that my body is tired — and I’ll get into bed in my apartment, close my laptop, lights off or mostly off, and then my brain just keeps going. It’s not even always one big dramatic thought. It’s more like I start mentally rechecking everything: work deadlines, emails I might have missed, whether I handled something correctly, then tuition payments, then class assignments, then I remember some other thing I need to do, and it just keeps looping.

And the frustrating part is I’ll tell myself, “Okay, you’re done for the day, you need to sleep,” but it doesn’t feel like there’s an off switch. I can be lying there for hours, not doing anything, not even on my computer anymore, but still kind of working in my head. And then even when I do finally fall asleep, it doesn’t feel restful. I wake up feeling like I never really turned off, like my mind was still running in the background the whole time.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences muscle tension or physical manifestations of anxiety that they may not have previously recognized or reported.
doctor.question: Do you notice any tightness in your muscles, especially in your neck, shoulders, or back, even when you're not doing anything physically strenuous?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking specifically about muscle tension in the neck, shoulders, or back, but the provided symptom profile does not include a muscle tension item.

patient.answer:
I’m not totally sure. I mean, I know what you mean in a general sense, like carrying tension in your shoulders or clenching without realizing it, but I haven’t really tracked that carefully.

I do sometimes notice I’m sort of… held stiffly, I guess, like I’ll realize I’m sitting at my desk with my shoulders up or my posture is really rigid. But I don’t know if I’d call it muscle tightness as a symptom, exactly, because I also sit at a computer a lot for work, so it’s hard for me to separate what’s just from being at my desk versus something else.

My neck and shoulders can feel tense at times, but I haven’t had this clear ongoing back or neck pain that I’ve been focused on. It’s more like I notice it after the fact, like, “Oh, I’m not relaxed,” but I wouldn’t say I’ve been doing anything physically strenuous when it happens. I just haven’t paid enough attention to say how often it’s happening.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences difficulty falling asleep due to racing thoughts, which is a key feature distinguishing Generalized Anxiety Disorder (F41.1) from other candidates.
doctor.question: Do you often have trouble falling asleep because your thoughts are racing or you can't shut them off, even when you're physically tired?

target_item.manifestation: I’m here because my sleep has basically fallen apart—I’ll lie in bed in my apartment for hours with my laptop closed, still mentally rechecking work deadlines, tuition payments, and class assignments, and even when I do sleep I wake up feeling like I never really turned off.
target_item.reason: The question is directly about trouble falling asleep and non-restorative sleep due to racing thoughts, which matches the sleep disturbance profile.

patient.answer:
Yes — definitely. Honestly, that’s one of the biggest reasons I’m here, because my sleep has basically fallen apart.

I’ll be lying in bed in my apartment, physically tired, laptop already closed, trying to be done for the day, and my mind just keeps going. I start rechecking things in my head — work deadlines, whether I missed something, tuition payments, class assignments — and it just loops. It’s like I can’t convince my brain that it’s allowed to stop.

Sometimes I’ll be there for hours, not even doing anything, just lying there thinking through the same things again and again. And then even when I do finally sleep, I wake up feeling like I never really turned off. It doesn’t feel restful.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences excessive daytime sleepiness or fatigue directly related to non-restorative sleep, a key feature distinguishing disorders like F51.0 (Nonorganic Sleep Disorder) from others.
doctor.question: Do you often feel excessively sleepy or struggle to stay awake during the day, even after what you think should have been a full night's sleep?

target_item.name: Fatigue
target_item.manifestation: By midafternoon at the office I feel completely drained, like even answering emails or walking to the subway takes effort, and resting on the weekend doesn’t seem to give me my energy back.
target_item.reason: The question is asking about daytime tiredness or sleepiness despite sleep, which most directly matches persistent fatigue not relieved by rest.

patient.answer:
Yeah, I do. I don’t know if I’d describe it as, like, literally nodding off at my desk all the time, but I feel really drained during the day. By midafternoon at the office, it’s like I hit this wall where even small things feel weirdly hard — answering emails, responding to messages, getting through whatever task I’m supposed to be doing.

And it’s not just “I could use a coffee” tired. It feels like my whole body and brain are running on empty. Even walking to the subway after work can feel like this huge effort, which sounds dramatic, but that’s how it feels in the moment.

I keep thinking if I could just catch up on sleep or rest on the weekend, I’d bounce back, but that doesn’t really happen. I’ll try to take it easy, and then Monday comes and I still feel like I’m starting the week already depleted. So yes, during the day I’m tired a lot — more drained than sleepy maybe, but definitely struggling to feel awake and functional.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences difficulty initiating or completing tasks due to low motivation or energy, which would support a depressive symptom pattern.
doctor.question: Do you find it hard to get started on tasks or responsibilities, even when you know you need to do them, because it feels like there’s no motivation or energy to begin?

target_item.name: Fatigue
target_item.manifestation: By midafternoon at the office I feel completely drained, like even answering emails or walking to the subway takes effort, and resting on the weekend doesn’t seem to give me my energy back.
target_item.reason: The question is asking about difficulty initiating tasks because of low motivation or energy, which most directly matches persistent fatigue and lack of energy.

patient.answer:
Yes, I do. It’s not even always that I don’t care about the task — like, I know the email needs an answer, or I know I need to start something for work — but by midafternoon at the office I feel so completely drained that starting feels weirdly impossible.

Even small things can feel like they require this huge amount of effort. I’ll be sitting there looking at my inbox thinking, “Okay, just answer this one message,” and it still feels like I have to force myself through mud to begin. And then by the time I’m leaving work, even something basic like walking to the subway can feel like more effort than it should.

I keep hoping that if I rest over the weekend, I’ll sort of reset and come back with more energy, but it doesn’t really work that way. I might take it easy, but I don’t feel restored enough. It’s like I’m starting from empty again.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences psychomotor agitation or slowed thinking, which could help differentiate between GAD, MDD, and Nonorganic Hypersomnia.
doctor.question: Do you find yourself moving more slowly than usual, or having trouble thinking clearly and making decisions, even when you're not physically tired?

target_item.name: Concentration_Difficulty
target_item.manifestation: I’ll stare at the same financial model or class reading for ages and realize I’ve reread the same paragraph five times without absorbing it, because my head is already off running through everything that could go wrong.
target_item.reason: The question is mainly about trouble thinking clearly and making decisions, which best matches difficulty concentrating or the mind going blank.

patient.answer:
Yes — mostly the thinking clearly and making decisions part. I’m not sure I’d say I’m physically moving in slow motion all the time, but mentally I get really stuck.

Like I’ll be looking at the same financial model at work, something I technically know how to review, and I’ll just… stare at it. I’ll read the same numbers or assumptions over and over and realize I haven’t actually taken anything in. Or with class readings, I’ll get through a paragraph and then notice I’ve basically reread the same paragraph five times and still couldn’t tell you what it said.

And it’s not because the material is impossible. It’s more like my mind is already somewhere else, running through everything that could go wrong — what if I miss something in the model, what if I fall behind, what if I don’t understand the reading well enough — and then I’m technically looking at the task, but I’m not really there. Even small decisions can take way longer than they should because I keep second-guessing what the “right” choice is.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences excessive worry about multiple areas of life, occurring more days than not, for at least six months, which is a key feature of generalized anxiety disorder (F41.1).
doctor.question: Have you been worrying about multiple things in your life, like work, school, or personal responsibilities, for more days than not over the past six months or longer?

target_item.name: Excessive_Anxiety_Worry
target_item.manifestation: My mind keeps jumping from whether I’m falling behind at work, to whether I’m wasting money on school, to whether my family will think I can’t handle things, and I treat every small issue like it could derail my whole future.
target_item.reason: The question is directly asking about persistent worry across multiple areas of life such as work, school, and responsibilities.

patient.answer:
Yes. Honestly, that’s probably the main thing that’s been going on. It’s not just one worry that comes and goes — my mind keeps jumping between different things, and it feels constant.

Like I’ll start out worrying that I’m falling behind at work, that I’m missing something important or not keeping up the way I’m supposed to. Then it turns into worrying about school and whether I’m wasting money on it, or whether I made the wrong choice trying to do all of this. And then somehow it becomes about my family and whether they’re going to think I can’t handle my life or that I’m not as capable as I should be.

It’s like every small issue feels bigger than it probably is. One email I haven’t answered, one assignment I’m unsure about, one expense I didn’t plan for — my brain treats it like it could derail everything, like my whole future is suddenly at risk. I know that sounds extreme when I say it out loud, but in the moment it feels very real. So yes, more days than not, for a long time now, I’m worrying about multiple things at once.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with persistent and excessive worry across multiple domains (work, school, personal responsibilities), difficulty controlling the worry, sleep disturbance, fatigue, impaired concentration, and restlessness, all of which have been present for more than six months. These symptoms align with Generalized Anxiety Disorder (F41.1). Adjustment Disorder with Anxiety (F43.22) and Nonorganic Insomnia (F51.0) were considered but are less likely due to the chronic, pervasive nature of the anxiety and the absence of a clear psychosocial stressor or isolated sleep complaint.
